analysis.one_liner: Requires online companies to protect, and stop misusing, the personal data they collect about users.
analysis.headline: The Data Care Act never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for the rest of the 117th Congress after being referred there in March 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written three basic duties into law for companies that collect data about people online: a duty to keep that data secure and warn users of breaches of sensitive data, a duty not to use it in ways that foreseeably harm or exploit the user, and a duty not to hand it off to anyone else unless that party accepts the same obligations. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and state attorneys general could also sue violators. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet or apps: their personal data — health information, precise location, financial details, biometrics, private messages — could no longer be used against them, sold onward to parties that ignore these duties, or left unsecured, with the FTC and state attorneys general empowered to sue violators and bar companies from making users sign away these rights.

how_it_helps.text: Online service providers must reasonably secure personal data and promptly tell users of breaches of their sensitive data, such as health records, financial account numbers, biometrics, and precise location [S3].

Providers cannot use personal data, or data derived from it, in ways that benefit the company to the detriment of the user, cause reasonably foreseeable material physical or financial harm, or would be unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable user [S3].

Providers cannot sell or share personal data with anyone unless that party contracts to the same duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality, and must audit those parties' data practices — extending the duties to data brokers and other recipients [S3].

The FTC enforces violations as unfair or deceptive practices — including over nonprofits and common carriers — and state attorneys general and state consumer protection officers can sue on behalf of residents, with civil penalties scaled to days of noncompliance or the number of end users harmed [S3].

The rights and remedies cannot be waived or limited by contract, so companies could not make users click away their protections, and the bill adds to rather than replaces existing federal and state privacy laws [S3].
The FTC may tailor or exempt requirements for small or low-risk providers, weighing size, complexity, and the sensitivity of data handled [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online service providers — from social media platforms and search engines to apps, ad-tech firms, and data brokers — bear the cost of securing data, auditing anyone they share it with, and forgoing profitable uses and sales of personal data that would harm users. Some cost may ultimately show up in prices or ad-supported services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-collecting tech companies and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The duty of loyalty turns on vague standards — what is 'reasonably foreseeable and material' harm or conduct 'unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable end user' — which could invite costly litigation and make compliance judgments uncertain for businesses of all sizes [S3].

The duties apply to any entity that collects individual identifying data, even incidentally, so small websites and startups face compliance burdens alongside the large platforms, though the FTC may exempt low-risk categories [S3].

Enforcement relies heavily on FTC rulemaking and case-by-case action, and state suits are paused while the FTC pursues the same defendant on the same facts, which could slow relief for affected users [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: consumers get legally enforceable duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality over their personal data, while data-driven companies give up profitable uses and sales of that data and take on security and audit costs. The vague 'highly offensive to a reasonable end user' standard and broad coverage of incidental data collectors are real design flaws that could have produced unpredictable litigation. But the FTC's flexibility to exempt small or low-risk providers, the preservation of stronger state laws, and the ban on contracting away rights make the design reasonably balanced; the main reason it never became law was not its content but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2021, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the Data Care Act of 2021 on March 23, 2021, joined by 17 other senators [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and was never taken up before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms, app makers, and data brokers that profit from collecting and monetizing personal data are better off, since no federal duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality were imposed; internet users are left with the same patchwork of sectoral and state privacy rules.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Care Act of 2021 establishing duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality for online service providers' handling of user data.

for.name: 18 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 17 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents, including Sens. Durbin, Klobuchar, Booker, Markey, Sanders, and Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from across the Senate Democratic caucus and its independent ally.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Majority party leadership controlling the Senate floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote at any point in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 17 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 2 independents — with no Republican support in the record, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Big tech platforms and app makers (search, social media, streaming)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from using or selling personal data in ways that foreseeably harm users and would require them to secure data and audit everyone they share it with. Their business models built on monetizing user data would be directly constrained.
As recipients of personal data, they would inherit the same duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality by contract, plus audits, ending unrestricted resale and sharing of consumer data.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and consumer protection offices
industries.note: The bill would give them explicit authority to sue violators on behalf of state residents, with civil penalties scaled to days of violation or users harmed — a new enforcement tool alongside the FTC.
